provenance.note: Bacillus PS3 ATP synthase, state 1 of three rotational states (PDB 6N2Y; cryo-EM at 3.0 Å; Guo, Suzuki and Rubinstein, eLife 2019). Prepared from a rigid-composite recipe: every chain is its own body with deposited coordinates; delta and the two b subunits keep backbone and C-beta atoms only. The model frame puts the rotor axis on +y through the origin, measured from the three deposited states (6N2Y, 6N2Z, 6N30). In animated chapters the 6N2Y gamma, epsilon and ten c subunits turn as one rigid body in idealised 120-degree steps, counterclockwise seen from the head, the direction of ATP synthesis. The generated poses are not deposited states: the deposited c-ring positions differ by about 108, 144 and 108 degrees, and the beta subunits keep their state-1 conformations.

chapters.title: The whole enzyme
chapters.caption: Bacillus PS3 ATP synthase, entry 6N2Y, cryo-EM at 3.0 Å. Three alpha and three beta subunits form the catalytic head. Below it, a ring of ten c subunits spans the membrane next to subunit a.

immersive.narration: Bacterial ATP synthase: catalytic head on top, membrane ring below.

chapters.title: Three parts, one rotor
chapters.caption: Gamma, epsilon and the c-ring turn together as one rotor; the peripheral stalk holds the head and subunit a in place. During ATP synthesis the rotor turns counterclockwise, seen from the head. This animation applies idealised 120-degree rotations to the 6N2Y rotor; its poses are not deposited states.

immersive.narration: Seen from the head, the rotor turns counterclockwise.

chapters.title: Protons drive the ring
chapters.caption: A proton enters from outside the cell through a half-channel in subunit a and binds Glu56 of a c subunit. The ring carries it almost a full turn to Arg169 of subunit a, where it leaves into the cell. In this state, Glu56 of the marked c subunit is 3.7 Å from Arg169.

immersive.narration: Each proton binds Glu56, turns with the ring, and leaves at Arg169.

chapters.title: Three catalytic sites
chapters.caption: In this state one beta subunit is closed on Mg-ADP, one is open with a putative phosphate modelled at its site, and one is held open by epsilon with its site empty. Each alpha subunit holds Mg-ATP at a non-catalytic site. Beta-TP, beta-DP and beta-E name the three positions around the rotor; in this inhibited state epsilon holds the beta-DP site open and empty (Guo et al. 2019).

immersive.narration: One site holds Mg-ADP, one a putative phosphate, one is empty.

chapters.title: Epsilon may block one direction
chapters.caption: Here epsilon reaches up into the head. It inserts between alpha-DP and beta-DP and holds beta-DP open. Its position suggests that a clash with beta-TP blocks the rotor turning in the direction that splits ATP, while the rotor stays free to turn in the direction that makes ATP. The maps show this position, not the turning (Guo et al., eLife 2019).

immersive.narration: Epsilon's position suggests it blocks the ATP-splitting turn.

chapters.title: Eleven nanometres apart
chapters.caption: Arg169, where protons leave the ring, is 11 nanometres from the ADP in the closed site. The rotor connects the two.

immersive.narration: Proton exit and closed catalytic site are 11 nanometres apart.

chapters.title: One full turn
chapters.caption: This animation turns the rotor in three idealised 120-degree steps; in the deposited states the c-ring positions differ by about 108, 144 and 108 degrees. Ten c subunits pass subunit a, so ten protons cross the membrane per turn.

immersive.narration: One full turn carries ten protons across the membrane.
